title: Al-Hayy, al-Qayyum
hook: the Living, the Self-Sustaining, on whom everything rests (2:255)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawakkul, trust, and al-Wakil, the Trustee. Your line was tie the camel, then trust.

Right now, something is holding you up. The chair. The floor under the chair. The building, the ground, the planet turning under all of it, and you're not thinking about any of it. You only notice what holds you when it wobbles. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once asked a companion, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, which verse of the Qur'an is the greatest. Ubayy answered with a verse whose first line names the Living, and the one who holds everything up. And the Prophet, the hadith in Sahih Muslim says, struck him on the chest, pleased, and congratulated him on his knowledge. Today, those two names, and the first of them is today's word: Al-Hayy.
screen: `WHAT'S HOLDING YOU UP?` → `THE GREATEST VERSE.` → `TWO NAMES.`

segments.voice: The verse is Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne, 2:255. In Pickthall's translation it begins: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him." The Alive is al-Hayy, from hayat, life. Muslim teachers put it this way: everything else that lives has borrowed its life and will give it back; al-Hayy's life isn't borrowed, with no start and no end. The Eternal is al-Qayyum, and here Pickthall picks one side of a rich word. It comes from q-w-m, to stand. Al-Qayyum is the One who stands by himself, needing nothing, and who keeps everything else standing: the Self-Subsisting, the Sustainer. Then the line that makes the names concrete: neither slumber nor sleep overtakes him. Every guard falls asleep. Every parent eventually dozes off in the chair by the crib. The one holding up the heavens and the earth never does. The verse goes on: his throne, his kursi, spans the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire him. That's why it's a bedtime verse: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever recites it on going to bed has a guardian from God through the night. In that picture, the sleeper can sleep because the Sustainer doesn't. And a du'a from the Prophet, in at-Tirmidhi, calls on the two names together: ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum, O Living, O Sustainer, by your mercy I seek help. Some scholars even suggested these two together are the greatest name of all.
screen: `AYAT AL-KURSI — 2:255.` · `AL-HAYY — LIFE NOT BORROWED.` · `AL-QAYYUM — KEEPS ALL STANDING.` · `NO SLUMBER, NO SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING RESTS ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Let your weight drop into the chair or the floor, and feel where you're touching it: your feet, your legs, your back. Then go one layer out, the ground under the floor, then the whole earth under that, and notice that you didn't have to hold any of it up. If you pray, you can say, quietly, ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum.
Al-Hayy. The Living, whose life is not borrowed, named together with al-Qayyum, the One who keeps everything standing. Today's word.
Your line: everything rests on him. The One holding it all up never sleeps. Rest well tonight.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after each obligatory prayer and when leaving the house, and call on God as ya Hayyu ya Qayyum in times of need.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is alive and eternal.
what it means: the Living, whose life isn't borrowed, and the one who stands alone and keeps all else standing, never sleeping.
what a scholar hears: qayyum is an intensive form from q-w-m, to stand. al-Hayy al-Qayyum appears in 2:255, 3:2 and 20:111, and some scholars proposed it as the greatest name.
recall: the one who provides for every creature

chat.says: Why do Muslims read Ayat al-Kursi before going to sleep?
options: It says God never sleeps, and a hadith promises a guardian through the night.
Because it's the shortest verse, so it's easy to say when tired.
Because it's a verse about dreams, asking God for good ones.
chat.meaning: Ayat al-Kursi says neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him, and a hadith in Bukhari gives whoever recites it at bedtime a guardian from God.
